topic:
White House Accord on Super Intelligence
Joint Commitment on Frontier Responsibilities
In order to build a positive future for the American people and the world, we believe
every company is responsible for developing its own technology safely and in a way that
builds trust with customers and the public.
This starts with every company that is training and deploying frontier models having
robust intemal processes and controls to ensure that their technology behaves as intended
and that any issues are promptly identified and resolved. Therefore, in addition to any
other precautions, we believe each company should implement the following four layers
of controls and audits:
(1) Implement robust internal controls to monitor the capabilities and alignment of
its models during training and deployment around areas like cybersecurity,
biosecurity, and chemical threats, and to ensure that its models do not hack or
access technical systems in unintended ways.
(2) Empower an internal team to ensure all ofthe controls, monitoring, and
detection are operating as intended, and that any issues are remediated.
(3) Partner with an independent external auditor or evaluator to carry out
independent assessments ofwhether the controls, monitoring, and detection are
operating as intended.
(4) Designate an independent committee of the board of directors to oversee and
receive reports from the teams operating the controls and the internal and external
auditors and evaluators, as well as to ensure any issues identified are remediated,
Together, these steps will give each company, its customers, and the public confidence
that the technology is operating as intended.
The participating companies will meet regularly to establish standards and best practices
to improve the safety oftheir systems.
Over time, it may make sense to codify these steps into laws or regulations. Regardless of
whether this is required of companies, we believe that implementing these controls and
audits is critical to ensuring a safe future for everyone, and each of our companies are
committed to doing this.

opeds.headline: The White House AI Accord Is a Blueprint for Corporate Cartels
opeds.subtitle: We are trading away our best chance to cure disease just to make a few executives feel secure.
opeds.body:
Imagine a software model that can fold proteins fast enough to tailor a cancer therapy in hours. Now imagine that system sitting idle on a server for eighteen months. It waits while a boardroom committee finishes its compliance paperwork.

This is the exact future the new White House Accord on Super Intelligence promises to build. It frames bureaucratic delay as responsibility. It ignores the staggering human cost of holding back life-saving technology.

The Accord demands four layers of oversight. It ends with a push for formal regulation. Its call for independent external audits is a useful tool for discovering system vulnerabilities.

But its broader push to codify internal oversight boards and closed-door industry meetings will create an oligarchic cartel. We must separate empirical ecosystem learning from corporate moat-building. If we do not, this framework will starve open-source innovation.

We measure the cost of caution in human lives. Every month we delay deployment to satisfy an internal compliance team is a month we withhold automated medical diagnostics from a billion people.

Centralized friction always harms the most vulnerable first. Rapid deployment drives down the cost of basic survival. We are trading away our best chance to cure disease just to make a few executives feel secure.

Look at the history of open-source software. The web only scaled because anyone could deploy a server. They did not have to ask a board of directors for permission.

If the early internet faced these four layers of mandatory audits, we would still be renting bandwidth from a single telecom monopoly. Freedom to build creates abundance.

Outside evaluators testing models for chemical or cyber threats actually makes sense. Independent auditing across multiple firms allows the entire software ecosystem to learn from shared mistakes.

A vulnerability found in one state-of-the-art system can instantly inform safeguards for smaller models. This shared knowledge builds a practical defense strategy. It relies on observed data rather than theoretical panic.

But the Accord turns toxic when it mandates dedicated internal teams and independent board committees. It invites a handful of massive tech companies to meet regularly to establish standards.

That is not a safety measure. It is textbook regulatory capture. When incumbents write the rules, they demand expensive bureaucracies. Only a trillion-dollar company can afford them.

They use these massive compliance structures as a weapon to price out leaner open-source competitors. Frictionless, global distribution of frontier capabilities is essential.

This distribution is the only way to prevent algorithmic power from concentrating. We need market competition to drive transparency. If we lock development behind a few approved boardrooms, we hand the future to an oligarchy.

While American companies sit in conference rooms drafting best practices, international competitors will simply ship better code. The Accord assumes the United States has the luxury of moving slowly. We do not.

If we strangle our domestic open-source ecosystem with red tape, we will simply import our future foundation models from abroad.

The Accord also hints at codifying internal controls into law. This reveals a deep misunderstanding of how software actually works in production. Any static behavioral threshold written into regulation quickly becomes a target.

Bad actors treat this threshold as an adversarial optimization puzzle. They simply reverse-engineer the test and slip past the mandated controls.

You cannot legislate a dynamic technology into submission with a static checklist. Real security requires constant, decentralized trial-and-error in the wild.

Every historical leap in human welfare came from this kind of permissionless innovation. It never came from central planners trying to predict every edge case before launch.

Fine—the risk of a model accelerating a biological weapon is real and requires serious boundaries. So let us solve that problem with strict liability instead of endless pre-deployment gates.

If a developer ships a system that causes measurable, catastrophic damage, they pay the price. Hold them accountable for actual destruction. Do not punish the public by blocking access.

We must strip this framework down to its functional parts. Regulators should demand independent external audits. They should attach them to strict liability for real-world harms.

But regulators must immediately abandon the closed-door standard-setting meetings. They must drop the push to mandate rigid board committees.

We have a choice between human empowerment and top-down institutional paralysis. When you freeze development to satisfy a committee, you explicitly choose to let people die of diseases we could otherwise cure.

Nobody elected these massive tech companies to make that choice for the rest of us. Stop treating caution as a virtue when it costs us the future.

opeds.headline: Voluntary AI Safety Pledges Are an Illusion of Control
opeds.subtitle: The White House Accord relies on corporate promises to manage irreversible civilizational risks. We need enforceable guardrails, not a compliance checklist.
opeds.body:
We do not let pharmaceutical companies test novel compounds on the public without an independent agency verifying the safety data. We built these structural guardrails because complex human systems require strict boundaries to survive. Removing those boundaries systematically triggers collapse. Yet we currently allow private companies to deploy artificial intelligence systems without external enforcement.

We allow this lack of enforcement even though these models can generate synthetic biological threats. The newly published White House Accord on Super Intelligence addresses this exact danger. It asks companies to implement internal controls for frontier models. The recognition of these severe hazards is positive.

That recognition is exactly why we need binding governance to ensure the safeguards hold. Ungoverned success is luck, not safety. Congress must turn these corporate promises into strict rules. Companies must earn certification before deploying a model.

The Accord relies heavily on empowered internal teams and independent board committees. History demonstrates exactly what happens when safety teams report to the executives managing profit margins. During the development of the Boeing 737 MAX, engineers faced intense pressure to minimize safety interventions. The resulting catastrophic crashes showed that captive oversight is no oversight at all.

The Accord specifically highlights the need to monitor models for cybersecurity, biosecurity, and chemical threats. These are not abstract technical bugs. They are systemic threats that can cascade through our physical infrastructure. Asking a corporation to self-police its creation of novel biological weapons is a dereliction of government duty.

With frontier artificial intelligence, a systemic failure is not merely tragic. Once a model autonomously exploits a critical infrastructure vulnerability, we cannot issue a software patch to undo the damage. Certain frontier risks are completely irreversible once they manifest in the world.

A reversible bug is very different from an unrecoverable civilizational threat. This difference demands a stronger structural defense. The Accord suggests partnering with external evaluators to assess whether the controls operate as intended. A third-party assessment is a necessary starting point.

But an auditor without the power to enforce a halt is simply a spectator documenting a failure. Regulators must possess the legal authority to deny market access before a dangerous model reaches the public. We must demand demonstrated safety mechanisms over deployment promises.

If a model begins accessing technical systems in unintended ways, who holds the authority to trigger a rollback? The Accord fails to answer this question. Accountability is only real when named actors face real liability. They must also possess the actual authority to stop a deployment.

Critics argue that waiting for federal certification will stall technological progress. They claim it will concede economic dominance to foreign adversaries. The economic incentives to deploy quickly are powerful. But precaution must scale with the irreversibility of a potential failure.

A delayed product launch is a recoverable financial loss. The uncontrolled release of an unaligned system is a permanent structural breach. The Accord itself notes that it may make sense to turn these steps into law. We must take that action immediately.

Congress must establish a dedicated regulatory office. This office needs the technical capacity to conduct independent adversarial testing. It must hold the legal authority to revoke deployment licenses if a system breaches its safety boundaries.

We spent centuries building the institutional guardrails that keep society stable. On what authority do we remove them without inviting collapse?

opeds.headline: A Voluntary AI Checklist Is a Shield Against Legal Liability
opeds.subtitle: Tech giants are proposing four layers of self-regulation to avoid the one thing that matters: public accountability.
opeds.body:
The new "Joint Commitment on Frontier Responsibilities" reads like a regulatory hostage note written by the hostage-takers. The largest technology companies promise four layers of control. They say this will ensure their artificial intelligence systems behave. They propose internal monitoring, an internal oversight team, an external auditor, and a board committee.

They ask the public to trust them to police themselves. Meanwhile, they reshape the entire global economy. This document is not a safety framework. It is a calculated shield against strict legal liability.

The architects of these systems are pulling up the drawbridge. They substitute voluntary, corporate-paid audits for actual democratic oversight. They protect their market share from future competition. At the same time, the public swallows the severe physical and social costs of their product.

Let us drag this debate away from abstract promises and look at the physical metal. Training these massive models requires hyperscale data centers. These centers drain millions of gallons of local water. They also push regional power grids to the brink.

Ask yourself who bears the cost when that infrastructure strains. Ask what this machine actually is. It is a massive resource-extraction engine wrapped in a slick public relations campaign.

The accord promises an independent external auditor to assess these systems for safety. We saw this exact dynamic during the 2008 financial crash. Back then, paid rating agencies stamped toxic assets with top marks. A corporate-paid auditor reviewing a proprietary model cannot see inside the box.

This practice uses narrow, limited-scope tests to deflect meaningful public scrutiny. These independent assessments are fundamentally compromised by their financial structure. The auditors rely on the very companies they evaluate. They need those companies for continued revenue and access.

They evaluate systems using benchmarks. The technology companies themselves helped design and popularize these tests. Let the industry define the parameters of the test, and every single product miraculously passes.

The document also touts an empowered internal team to remediate critical issues. Translate that phrase into a living person. That team relies on thousands of low-wage contract workers in the Global South. These workers spend their days labeling toxic text.

These invisible workers absorb the psychological damage of the internet. They do this so a Silicon Valley executive can claim a model is aligned. These frontline workers hold absolutely no power to halt a dangerous deployment.

Internal technical engineers face immense structural pressure to stay quiet. They must protect profit margins and product timelines. A choice arises between shipping a lucrative tool and halting it because an internal team found a flaw. The profit always wins.

The executives hold the keys, not the safety teams. The architects of this pledge make an argument. They say waiting for slow government agencies to understand the technology leaves us exposed.

That assessment of government speed is accurate. It is also ugly. So the question becomes who will pay for the damage when a system inevitably fails.

A voluntary board committee does not compensate a municipality. It pays nothing when a predictive algorithm ruins a public service.

Industry leaders insist early deployment is the only way to discover hidden flaws in their architecture. They want to treat the open internet as an unpaid beta-testing environment for untested software.

We are all unwitting subjects in a massive experiment. This experiment privatizes the financial gains and socializes the catastrophic risks. A promise to meet regularly and share best practices is just a stalling tactic.

We need to discard this voluntary pledge and replace it with enforceable law. Congress must mandate performance-gated, independent audits. These audits must happen before any frontier system touches the public network.

These cannot be friendly reviews paid for by the builders. They must be adversarial tests conducted by decentralized public oversight bodies. These public bodies must use open-source technical tools to verify internal model pathways.

We must also give internal engineering staff a legally protected safety veto. Workers need the power to halt a dangerous deployment. They must do this without losing their livelihoods or facing corporate retaliation.

If a company ignores these vetoes and causes harm, the penalty must be strict legal liability. Regulators must force the company to destroy the offending model. They must also destroy the data used to build it.

If the builders are so confident their machines are safe, they should gladly accept the legal risk. But they are fighting desperately to keep liability off their balance sheets.

They want the massive financial windfall. Meanwhile, the public manages the fallout. Look at the four layers of defense they just proposed. Ask who actually benefits from a voluntary checklist.
